{{Short description|Type of 2D conformal field theory}}
{{Distinguish|Wess–Zumino model}}
In [[theoretical physics]] and [[mathematics]], a '''Wess–Zumino–Witten''' ('''WZW''') '''model''', also called a '''Wess–Zumino–Novikov–Witten model''', is a type of [[two-dimensional conformal field theory]] named after [[Julius Wess]], [[Bruno Zumino]], [[Sergei Novikov (mathematician)|Sergei Novikov]] and [[Edward Witten]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Wess | first1 = J. | last2 = Zumino | first2 = B. | doi = 10.1016/0370-2693(71)90582-X | title = Consequences of anomalous ward identities | journal = Physics Letters B | volume = 37 | pages = 95–97 | year = 1971 | issue = 1 |bibcode = 1971PhLB...37...95W | url = https://cds.cern.ch/record/486885/files/CM-P00058941.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Witten | first1 = E. | title = Global aspects of current algebra | doi = 10.1016/0550-3213(83)90063-9 | journal = Nuclear Physics B | volume = 223 | issue = 2 | pages = 422–432| year = 1983 |bibcode = 1983NuPhB.223..422W }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Witten | first1 = E. | title = Non-abelian bosonization in two dimensions | doi = 10.1007/BF01215276 | journal = Communications in Mathematical Physics | volume = 92 | issue = 4 | pages = 455–472 | year = 1984 |bibcode = 1984CMaPh..92..455W | s2cid = 122018499 | url = http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1103940923 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=Novikov, S. P. | title=Multivalued functions and functionals. An analogue of the Morse theory | journal= Sov. Math., Dokl. | volume=24 | pages=222–226 | year=1981}}; {{Cite journal | last1 = Novikov | first1 = S. P. | title = The Hamiltonian formalism and a many-valued analogue of Morse theory | doi = 10.1070/RM1982v037n05ABEH004020 | journal = Russian Mathematical Surveys | volume = 37 | issue = 5 | pages = 1–9 | year = 1982 |bibcode = 1982RuMaS..37....1N | s2cid = 250867649 }}</ref> A WZW model is associated to a [[Lie group]] (or [[supergroup (physics)|supergroup]]), and its symmetry algebra is the [[affine Lie algebra]] built from the corresponding [[Lie algebra]] (or [[Lie superalgebra]]). By extension, the name WZW model is sometimes used for any conformal field theory whose symmetry algebra is an affine Lie algebra.<ref name="BYB"/>

==Action==

===Definition===

For <math>\Sigma</math> a [[Riemann surface]], <math>G</math> a [[Lie group]], and <math>k</math> a (generally complex) number, let us define the '''<math>G</math>-WZW model on <math>\Sigma</math> at the level <math>k</math>'''. The model is a [[nonlinear sigma model]] whose [[action (physics)|action]] is a functional of a field <math>\gamma:\Sigma \to G</math>:

:<math>S_k(\gamma)= -\frac{k}{8\pi} \int_{\Sigma} d^2x\, \mathcal{K} \left (\gamma^{-1} \partial^\mu \gamma, \gamma^{-1} \partial_\mu \gamma \right ) + 2\pi k S^{\mathrm WZ}(\gamma).</math>

Here, <math>\Sigma</math> is equipped with a flat [[Euclidean metric]], <math>\partial_\mu</math> is the [[partial derivative]], and <math>\mathcal{K}</math> is the [[Killing form]] on the [[Lie algebra]] of <math>G</math>. The '''Wess–Zumino term''' of the action is

:<math>S^{\mathrm WZ}(\gamma) = -\frac{1}{48\pi^2} \int_{\mathbf{B}^3} d^3y\, \epsilon^{ijk} \mathcal{K} \left( \gamma^{-1} \partial_i \gamma, \left[\gamma^{-1} \partial_j \gamma, \gamma^{-1} \partial_k \gamma \right]\right).</math>

Here <math>\epsilon^{ijk}</math> is the [[completely anti-symmetric tensor]], and <math>[.,.]</math> is the [[Lie bracket]]. 
The Wess–Zumino term is an integral over a three-dimensional manifold <math>\mathbf{B}^3</math> whose boundary is <math>\partial \mathbf{B}^3 = \Sigma</math>.

===Topological properties of the Wess–Zumino term===

For the Wess–Zumino term to make sense, we need the field <math>\gamma</math> to have an extension to <math>\mathbf{B}^3</math>. This requires the [[homotopy group]] <math>\pi_2(G)</math> to be trivial, which is the case in particular for any compact Lie group <math>G</math>.

The extension of a given <math>\gamma:\Sigma \to G</math> to <math>\mathbf{B}^3</math> is in general not unique. 
For the WZW model to be well-defined, <math>e^{iS_k(\gamma)}</math> 
should not depend on the choice of the extension. 
The Wess–Zumino term is invariant under small deformations of <math>\gamma</math>, and only depends on its [[homotopy class]]. 
Possible homotopy classes are controlled by the homotopy group <math>\pi_3(G)</math>.

For any compact, connected [[simple Lie group]] <math>G</math>, we have <math>\pi_3(G)=\mathbb{Z}</math>, and different extensions of <math>\gamma</math> lead to values of <math>S^{\mathrm WZ}(\gamma)</math> that differ by integers. Therefore, they lead to the same value of <math>e^{iS_k(\gamma)}</math> provided the level obeys

:<math> k \in \mathbb{Z}.</math>

Integer values of the level also play an important role in the representation theory of the model's symmetry algebra, which is an [[affine Lie algebra]]. If the level is a positive integer, the affine Lie algebra has unitary highest weight [[representation theory|representations]] with highest [[weight (representation theory)|weight]]s that are dominant integral. Such representations decompose into finite-dimensional subrepresentations with respect to the subalgebras spanned by each [[Simple root (root system)|simple root]], the corresponding negative root and their commutator, which is a [[Cartan matrix|Cartan generator]].

In the case of the noncompact simple Lie group [[SL2(R)|<math>\mathrm{SL}(2,\R)</math>]],
the homotopy group <math>\pi_3(\mathrm{SL}(2,\R))</math> is trivial, and the level is not constrained to be an integer.<ref name="MO">{{Cite journal | last1 = Maldacena | first1 = J. | last2 = Ooguri | first2 = H. | doi = 10.1063/1.1377273 | title = Strings in AdS<sub>3</sub> and the SL(2,R) WZW model. I: The spectrum | journal = Journal of Mathematical Physics | volume = 42 | issue = 7 | pages = 2929–2960 | year = 2001 |arxiv = hep-th/0001053 |bibcode = 2001JMP....42.2929M | s2cid = 8841465 }}</ref>

===Geometrical interpretation of the Wess–Zumino term===

If ''e<sub>a</sub>'' are the basis vectors for the [[Lie algebra]], then <math>\mathcal{K} (e_a, [e_b, e_c])</math> are the [[structure constants]] of the Lie algebra. The structure constants are completely anti-symmetric, and thus they define a [[alternating form|3-form]] on the [[group manifold]] of ''G''. Thus, the integrand above is just the [[pullback (differential geometry)|pullback]] of the harmonic 3-form to the ball <math>\mathbf{B}^3.</math> Denoting the harmonic 3-form by ''c'' and the pullback by <math>\gamma^*,</math> one then has

:<math>S^{\mathrm WZ}(\gamma) = \int_{\mathbf{B}^3} \gamma^{*} c.</math>

This form leads directly to a topological analysis of the WZ term.

Geometrically, this term describes the [[Torsion tensor|torsion]] of the respective manifold.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Braaten | first1 = E. | last2 = Curtright | first2 = T. L. | last3 = Zachos | first3 = C. K. | doi = 10.1016/0550-3213(85)90053-7 | title = Torsion and geometrostasis in nonlinear sigma models | journal = Nuclear Physics B | volume = 260 | issue = 3–4 | pages = 630 | year = 1985 |bibcode = 1985NuPhB.260..630B }}</ref> The presence of this torsion compels [[teleparallelism]] of the manifold, and thus trivialization of the torsionful [[Affine connection|curvature tensor]]; and hence arrest of the renormalization flow, an [[infrared fixed point]] of the [[renormalization group]], a phenomenon termed '''geometrostasis'''.

==Symmetry algebra==

===Generalised group symmetry===

The Wess–Zumino–Witten model is not only symmetric under global transformations by a group element in <math> G </math>, but also has a much richer symmetry. This symmetry is often called the <math> G(z) \times G(\bar{z}) </math> symmetry.<ref>Zamolodchikov, A. B.; Knizhnik, B. G. (1984). "Алгебра токов и двумерная модель Весса-Зумино". ''Nuclear Physics B.''  '''247''': 83-103.</ref> Namely, given any holomorphic <math>G</math>-valued function <math>\Omega(z)</math>, and any other (completely independent of <math>\Omega(z)</math>) antiholomorphic <math>G</math>-valued function <math>\bar{\Omega}(\bar{z})</math>, where we have identified <math> z=x+iy </math> and <math> \bar{z} = x-iy </math> in terms of the Euclidean space coordinates <math>x,y</math>, the following symmetry holds:

:<math> S_k (\gamma) = S_k (\Omega \gamma \bar{\Omega}^{-1} ) </math>

One way to prove the existence of this symmetry is through repeated application of the Polyakov–Wiegmann identity regarding products of <math>G</math>-valued fields:

:<math> S_k (\alpha \beta^{-1}) = S_k(\alpha) + S_k(\beta^{-1}) + \frac{k}{16\pi^2}\int d^2 x \textrm{Tr}(\alpha^{-1} \partial_{\bar{z}} \alpha \beta^{-1} \partial_{z} \beta)  </math>

The holomorphic and anti-holomorphic currents <math> J(z) = - \frac{1}{2}k (\partial_z \gamma) \gamma^{-1} </math> and <math> \bar{J}(\bar{z}) = - \frac{1}{2} k \gamma^{-1} \partial_{\bar{z}} \gamma </math> are the conserved currents associated with this symmetry. The singular behaviour of the products of these currents with other quantum fields determine how those fields transform under infinitesimal actions of the <math> G(z) \times G(\bar{z})</math> group.

===Affine Lie algebra===

Let <math>z</math> be a local complex coordinate  on <math>\Sigma</math>, 
<math> \{t^a\} </math> an orthonormal basis (with respect to the [[Killing form]])  of the Lie algebra of <math>G </math>, and <math> J^a(z) </math> the quantization of the field  <math> \mathcal{K}(t^a,\partial_z g g^{-1}) </math>. We have the following [[operator product expansion]]:

: <math> J^a(z) J^b(w) = \frac{k\delta^{ab}}{(z - w)^2} + \frac{i f^{ab}_c J^c(w)}{z - w} + \mathcal{O}(1), </math>

where <math>f^{ab}_c</math> are the coefficients such that <math>[t^a,t^b] = f^{ab}_c t^c</math>. 
Equivalently, if <math> J^a(z) </math> is expanded in modes

: <math> J^a(z)  = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} J_n^a z^{-n-1}, </math>

then the [[current algebra]] generated by <math> \{J_n^a\} </math> is the [[affine Lie algebra]] associated to the Lie algebra of <math>G</math>, with a level that coincides with the level <math>k</math> of the WZW model.<ref name="BYB">{{citation|first1=P.|last1= Di Francesco|first2=P. |last2=Mathieu|first3=D. |last3=Sénéchal|title=Conformal Field Theory|publisher=Springer-Verlag| year=1997|isbn=0-387-94785-X}}</ref> 
If <math>\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Lie}(G)</math>, the notation for the affine Lie algebra is <math> \hat{\mathfrak{g}}_k</math>.
The commutation relations of the affine Lie algebra are

: <math> [J^a_n,J^b_m] = f^{ab}_c J^c_{m+n} + kn\delta^{ab}\delta_{n+m,0}. </math>

This affine Lie algebra is the chiral symmetry algebra associated to the left-moving currents <math> \mathcal{K}(t^a,\partial_z g g^{-1}) </math>. A second copy of the same affine Lie algebra is associated to the right-moving currents <math>\mathcal{K}(t^a, g^{-1}\partial_{\bar z} g) </math>. The generators <math>\bar J^a(z)</math> of that second copy are antiholomorphic. The full symmetry algebra of the WZW model is the product of the two copies of the affine Lie algebra.

===Sugawara construction===

The [[Hirotaka Sugawara|Sugawara]] construction is an embedding of the [[Virasoro algebra]] into the universal enveloping algebra of the affine Lie algebra. The existence of the embedding shows that WZW models are conformal field theories. Moreover, it leads to [[Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations]] for correlation functions.

The Sugawara construction is most concisely written at the level of the currents: <math> J^a(z) </math> for the affine Lie algebra, and the [[Two-dimensional conformal field theory#Energy–momentum tensor|energy-momentum tensor]] <math>T(z)</math> for the Virasoro algebra:

: <math> T(z) = \frac{1}{2(k + h^{\vee})} \sum_a : J^a J^a : (z), </math>

where the <math> : </math> denotes normal ordering, and <math>h^{\vee}</math> is the [[Coxeter element|dual Coxeter number]]. By using the [[Operator product expansion|OPE]] of the currents and a version of [[Wick's theorem]] one may deduce that the OPE of <math> T(z) </math> with itself is given by<ref name="BYB"/>

:<math> T(y)T(z) = \frac{\frac{c}{2}}{(y-z)^4} + \frac{2T(z)}{(y-z)^2} + \frac{\partial T(z)}{y-z} + \mathcal{O}(1),</math>

which is equivalent to the Virasoro algebra's commutation relations. The central charge of the Virasoro algebra is given in terms of the level <math>k</math> of the affine Lie algebra by

:<math> c = \frac{k\mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{g})}{k + h^{\vee}}.</math>

At the level of the generators of the affine Lie algebra, the Sugawara construction reads

:<math> 
L_{n\neq 0} = \frac{1}{2(k + h^{\vee})} \sum_a \sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}} J^a_{n-m} J^a_m, 
</math> 
:<math>
L_0 = \frac{1}{2(k + h^{\vee})} \left(2\sum_a \sum_{m=1}^\infty J^a_{-m}J^a_m + J^0_aJ^0_a\right).
</math>

where the generators <math>L_n</math> of the Virasoro algebra are the modes of the energy-momentum tensor, <math>T(z) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} L_nz^{-n-2}</math>.

==Spectrum==
===WZW models with compact, simply connected groups===
If the Lie group <math>G</math> is compact and simply connected, then the WZW model is rational and diagonal: rational because the spectrum is built from a (level-dependent) finite set of irreducible representations of the affine Lie algebra called the integrable [[highest weight representation]]s, and diagonal because a representation of the left-moving algebra is coupled with the same representation of the right-moving algebra.<ref name="BYB"/>

For example, the spectrum of the <math>SU(2)</math> WZW model at level <math>k\in\mathbb{N}</math> is 
:<math> \mathcal{S}_k = \bigoplus_{j=0,\frac12,1,\dots, \frac{k}{2}} \mathcal{R}_j\otimes \bar{\mathcal{R}}_j\ ,
</math>
where <math> \mathcal{R}_j</math> is the affine highest weight representation of spin <math>j</math>: a representation generated by a state <math>|v\rangle</math> such that 
:<math> 
J^a_{n<0}|v\rangle = J^-_0|v\rangle=0\ ,
</math>
where <math>J^-</math> is the current that corresponds to a generator <math>t^-</math> of the Lie algebra of <math>SU(2)</math>.

===WZW models with other types of groups===

If the group <math>G</math> is compact but not simply connected, the WZW model is rational but not necessarily diagonal. For example, the <math>SO(3)</math> WZW model exists for even integer levels <math>k\in 2\mathbb{N}</math>, and its spectrum is a non-diagonal combination of finitely many integrable highest weight representations.<ref name="BYB"/>

If the group <math>G</math> is not compact, the WZW model is non-rational. Moreover, its spectrum may include non highest weight representations. For example, the spectrum of the <math>SL(2,\mathbb{R})</math> WZW model is built from highest weight representations, plus their images under the spectral flow automorphisms of the affine Lie algebra.<ref name="MO"/>

If <math>G</math> is a [[supergroup (physics)|supergroup]], the spectrum may involve representations that do not factorize as tensor products of representations of the left- and right-moving symmetry algebras. This occurs for example in the case <math>G= GL(1|1)</math>,<ref>V. Schomerus, H. Saleur, "The GL(1|1) WZW model: From supergeometry to logarithmic CFT", [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0510032 arxiv:hep-th/0510032]</ref>
and also in more complicated supergroups such as <math>G=PSU(1,1|2)</math>.<ref name="GQS">G. Gotz, T. Quella, V. Schomerus, "The WZNW model on PSU(1,1|2)", [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0610070 arxiv:hep-th/0610070]</ref>
Non-factorizable representations are responsible for the fact that the corresponding WZW models are [[logarithmic conformal field theory|logarithmic conformal field theories]].

===Other theories based on affine Lie algebras===

The known conformal field theories based on affine Lie algebras are not limited to WZW models.
For example, in the case of the affine Lie algebra of the <math>SU(2)</math> WZW model, modular invariant torus partition functions obey an ADE classification, where the <math>SU(2)</math> WZW model accounts for the A series only.<ref>Andrea Cappelli and Jean-Bernard Zuber (2010), [http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/A-D-E_Classification_of_Conformal_Field_Theories "A-D-E Classification of Conformal Field Theories"], Scholarpedia 5(4):10314.</ref> The D series corresponds to the <math>SO(3)</math> WZW model, and the E series does not correspond to any WZW model.

Another example is the <math>H_3^+</math> model. This model is based on the same symmetry algebra as the <math>SL(2,\mathbb{R})</math> WZW model, to which it is related by [[Wick rotation]]. However, the <math>H_3^+</math> is not strictly speaking a WZW model, as <math>H_3^+ =SL(2,\mathbb{C})/SU(2)</math> is not a group, but a coset.<ref>K. Gawedzki, "Non-Compact WZW Conformal Field Theories", [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9110076 arxiv:hep-th/9110076]</ref>

==Fields and correlation functions==
===Fields===
Given a simple [[Lie algebra representation|representation]] <math>\rho</math> of the Lie algebra of <math>G</math>, an '''affine primary field''' <math>\Phi^\rho(z)</math> is a field that takes values in the representation space of <math>\rho</math>, such that 
:<math>
J^a(y) \Phi^\rho(z) = -\frac{\rho(t^a)\Phi^\rho(z)}{y-z} + O(1)\ .
</math>
An affine primary field is also a [[primary field]] for the Virasoro algebra that results from the Sugawara construction. The conformal dimension of the affine primary field is given in terms of the quadratic Casimir <math>C_2(\rho)</math> of the representation <math>\rho</math> (i.e. the eigenvalue of the quadratic [[Casimir element]] <math>K_{ab}t^at^b</math> where <math>K_{ab}</math> is the inverse of the matrix <math>\mathcal{K}(t^a,t^b)</math> of the Killing form) by 
:<math>
\Delta_\rho = \frac{C_2(\rho)}{2(k+h^\vee)}\ . 
</math>
For example, in the <math>SU(2)</math> WZW model, the conformal dimension of a primary field of [[Spin (physics)|spin]] <math>j</math> is 
:<math>\Delta_j = \frac{j(j+1)}{k+2} \ .</math>

By the state-field correspondence, affine primary fields correspond to '''affine primary states''', which are the highest weight states of [[highest weight representation]]s of the affine Lie algebra.

===Correlation functions===
If the group <math>G</math> is compact, the spectrum of the WZW model is made of highest weight representations, and all correlation functions can be deduced from correlation functions of affine primary fields via [[Ward identities]].

If the Riemann surface <math>\Sigma</math> is the [[Riemann sphere]], correlation functions of affine primary fields obey [[Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations]]. On Riemann surfaces of higher genus, correlation functions obey '''Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov–Bernard equations''', which involve derivatives not only of the fields' positions, but also of the surface's moduli.<ref>G. Felder, C. Wieczerkowski, "Conformal blocks on elliptic curves and the Knizhnik--Zamolodchikov--Bernard equations", [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9411004 arxiv:hep-th/9411004]</ref>

==Gauged WZW models==
Given a Lie subgroup <math>H\subset G</math>, the <math>G/H</math> '''gauged WZW model''' (or '''coset model''') is a nonlinear sigma model whose target space is the quotient <math>G/H</math> for the [[adjoint action]] of <math>H</math> on <math>G</math>. This gauged WZW model is a conformal field theory, whose symmetry algebra is a quotient of the two affine Lie algebras of the <math>G</math> and <math>H</math> WZW models, and whose central charge is the difference of their central charges.

==Applications==

The WZW model whose Lie group is the [[universal cover]] of the group <math>\mathrm{SL}(2,\R)</math> has been used by [[Juan Maldacena]] and [[Hirosi Ooguri]] to describe bosonic [[string theory]] on the three-dimensional [[anti-de Sitter space]] <math>AdS_3</math>.<ref name="MO"/> Superstrings on <math>AdS_3\times S^3</math> are described by the WZW model on the supergroup <math>PSU(1,1|2)</math>, or a deformation thereof if [[Ramond–Ramond field|Ramond-Ramond]] flux is turned on.<ref>N. Berkovits, C. Vafa, E. Witten, "Conformal Field Theory of AdS Background with Ramond-Ramond Flux", [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9902098 arxiv:hep-th/9902098]</ref><ref name="GQS"/>

WZW models and their deformations have been proposed for describing 
the plateau transition in the integer [[quantum Hall effect]].<ref>M. Zirnbauer, "The integer quantum Hall plateau transition is a current algebra after all", [https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.12555 arXiv:1805.12555]</ref>

The <math>SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)</math> gauged WZW model has an interpretation in [[string theory]] as [[Edward Witten|Witten]]'s two-dimensional Euclidean black hole.<ref name="Witten1991">{{cite journal|last1=Witten|first1=Edward|title=String theory and black holes|journal=Physical Review D|volume=44|issue=2|year=1991|pages=314–324|issn=0556-2821|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.44.314|pmid=10013884 |bibcode=1991PhRvD..44..314W }}</ref>
The same model also describes certain two-dimensional statistical systems at criticality, such as the critical antiferromagnetic [[Potts model]].<ref>N. Robertson, J. Jacobsen, H. Saleur, "Conformally invariant boundary conditions in the antiferromagnetic Potts model and the <math>SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)</math> sigma model", [https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07565 arXiv:1906.07565]</ref>
